subject: Pathology
topic: Celiac Disease Lamina Propria Antigen Processing Dynamics
stem: A 32-year-old woman presents to the gastroenterology clinic with a 9-month history of foul-smelling, bulky, floating stools, postprandial abdominal bloating, and an unintentional 7-kg weight loss. She also reports progressive fatigue and easy bruising. Physical examination reveals an underweight woman with temporal wasting, pallor, and a symmetrically distributed, intensely pruritic eruption composed of grouped vesicles and excoriations over the extensor surfaces of both elbows and knees (dermatitis herpetiformis). Laboratory evaluation reveals: hemoglobin 9.4 g/dL, MCV 72 fL, serum ferritin 8 ng/mL, serum calcium 8.1 mg/dL, and elevated prothrombin time (INR 1.6, responsive to parenteral phytonadione). Serological screening reveals high-titer anti-tissue transglutaminase (anti-tTG) IgA antibodies with normal total serum IgA. Upper endoscopy reveals scalloping and flattening of mucosal folds in the second portion of the duodenum. Microscopic examination of duodenal mucosal biopsies demonstrates marked intraepithelial lymphocytosis (> 40 lymphocytes per 100 enterocytes), elongated hyperplastic crypts, and total atrophy and blunting of duodenal villi. Which of the following cellular or biochemical events in the lamina propria is fundamentally required for the pathogenic presentation of dietary antigens to mucosal CD4+ T lymphocytes?

options.text: Enzymatic conversion of neutral glutamine residues into negatively charged glutamic acid, enabling high-affinity anchoring into HLA-DQ2 and HLA-DQ8 binding grooves
options.explanation: The patient presents with celiac disease (gluten-sensitive enteropathy) with classic malabsorption of fat-soluble vitamins (vitamins A, D, E, K), iron-deficiency anemia, dermatitis herpetiformis, and pathognomonic duodenal histopathology (intraepithelial lymphocytosis, crypt hyperplasia, complete villous blunting). Dietary gluten contains gliadin, a polypeptide unusually rich in proline and glutamine residues that renders it resistant to complete luminal degradation by gastric pepsin and pancreatic endopeptidases. Resistant 33-mer gliadin fragments cross the epithelial barrier into the lamina propria via transcellular or paracellular routes. In the lamina propria, the endogenous calcium-dependent enzyme tissue transglutaminase (tTG / TG2) performs a critical post-translational modification: it DEAMIDATES neutral glutamine residues into negatively charged GLUTAMIC ACID. This charge conversion is the central pathophysiological trigger of the disease: negatively charged glutamic acid residues fit with high electrostatic affinity into the positively charged, basic peptide-binding pockets of HLA-DQ2 (or HLA-DQ8) molecules on mucosal dendritic cells. Presentation of deamidated gliadin drives clonal expansion of pathogenic CD4+ Th1 cells that secrete interferon-gamma, while enterocyte stress induces IL-15 expression, activating CD8+ intraepithelial lymphocytes to mediate perforin/granzyme-dependent enterocyte lysis.

options.text: Cleavage of the invariant chain (CLIP) by mucosal HLA-DM facilitating exogenous peptide exchange within late endosomal compartments
options.explanation: HLA-DM-mediated removal of CLIP is the standard, universal pathway for all exogenous antigen presentation by MHC class II molecules in all antigen-presenting cells; it does not confer the specific charge alteration of gliadin that initiates celiac autoimmunity.

options.text: Ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation of cytosolic peptides for TAP-dependent transport into the endoplasmic reticulum
options.explanation: Ubiquitination and TAP-mediated transport into the ER is the pathway for cytosolic endogenous peptide presentation on MHC class I molecules to CD8+ T cells, whereas celiac pathogenesis is driven by lamina propria MHC class II (HLA-DQ2/DQ8) CD4+ T-cell presentation.

options.text: Translocation of intact dietary polypeptide complexes across enterocyte membranes via neonatal Fc receptor-mediated transcytosis
options.explanation: The neonatal Fc receptor (FcRn) mediates transcellular transport of IgG antibodies across mucosal barriers, not the critical enzymatic modification of dietary gliadin peptides.

options.text: Retrograde transport of intact gliadin oligomers via the Golgi apparatus into the rough endoplasmic reticulum for retrograde secretion
options.explanation: Retrograde Golgi-to-ER translocation is utilized by AB bacterial toxins (e.g., cholera toxin, Shiga toxin), not dietary antigen presentation in celiac enteropathy.

subject: Microbiology
topic: Whipple Disease Tropheryma Whipplei Foamy Macrophage Pathology
stem: A 52-year-old Caucasian male agricultural worker presents to the clinic with an 8-month history of severe, watery diarrhea, foul-smelling stools, abdominal cramping, and an unintentional 14-kg weight loss. Over the preceding 5 years, he experienced recurrent episodes of migratory, non-deforming pain and swelling in his knees, wrists, and ankles that was diagnosed as seronegative arthritis and treated with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. Over the past 2 months, his family has noticed progressive memory loss, confusion, and rhythmic, synchronized, involuntary twitching of his facial muscles and jaw when chewing (oculofacial myorhythmia). Physical examination reveals a cachectic man with generalized brown-gray hyperpigmentation of sun-exposed skin, generalized non-tender peripheral lymphadenopathy, and a grade 2/6 systolic ejection murmur. Laboratory evaluation demonstrates iron-deficiency anemia (hemoglobin 8.8 g/dL), hypoalbuminemia (albumin 2.3 g/dL), and steatorrhea on 72-hour fecal fat testing. Upper endoscopy reveals pale yellow, shaggy, plaque-like mucosal patches throughout the duodenal mucosa. Endoscopic duodenal mucosal biopsy is performed. Microscopic examination demonstrates marked expansion of the intestinal lamina propria by dense sheets of distended, foamy macrophages that are completely packed with granular, rod-shaped material that stains bright magenta-pink with Periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) and remains strongly positive following treatment with diastase. Ziehl-Neelsen acid-fast staining of these macrophages is negative. Which of the following microbiological agents is the causative organism of this patient’s disease?

options.text: Mycobacterium avium-intracellulare complex, an acid-fast positive intracellular mycobacterium
options.explanation: Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC) causes identical PAS-positive foamy macrophage infiltration in the small bowel in AIDS (CD4 < 50), but MAC is strongly Ziehl-Neelsen acid-fast positive, whereas T. whipplei is acid-fast negative.

options.text: Tropheryma whipplei, a Gram-positive actinobacterium that persists within macrophage phagolysosomes
options.explanation: The patient has Whipple disease, a rare chronic multi-system granulomatous-like infection caused by the fastidious, rod-shaped, Gram-positive actinobacterium Tropheryma whipplei. Whipple disease predominantly affects Caucasian men in their 40s to 60s who work in agriculture, soil, or sewage environments. Pathogenesis involves defective host cellular immunity allowing the bacterium to survive and proliferate within macrophage phagolysosomes without being cleared. Hallmark clinical presentation includes the "CAN" triad: (1) Cardiac involvement (culture-negative endocarditis, pericarditis); (2) Arthralgias / arthritis (migratory, non-erosive oligo- or polyarthritis that typically precedes gastrointestinal complaints by 5–10 years); (3) Neurologic deficits (progressive dementia, supranuclear gaze palsy, and pathognomonic oculomasticatory or oculofacial myorhythmia); and (4) Gastrointestinal malabsorption (severe steatorrhea, weight loss, abdominal pain, hyperpigmentation, and lymphadenopathy). Duodenal mucosal biopsy is diagnostic: it demonstrates distorted, widened intestinal villi with lamina propria expanded by dense sheets of foamy macrophages stuffed with intracellular, granular, rod-shaped bacteria. Because the bacterial cell wall contains abundant peptidoglycans, it stains intensely positive with Periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) and is completely resistant to digestion by diastase (PAS-positive, diastase-resistant). Crucially, acid-fast staining is negative, ruling out Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC in AIDS patients also produces PAS-positive foamy macrophages, but MAC is strongly acid-fast positive). Treatment requires intravenous ceftriaxone for 2 to 4 weeks followed by maintenance oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for 1 full year to eradicate intracellular organisms and prevent fatal central nervous system relapse.

options.text: Giardia duodenalis, a flagellated pear-shaped protozoan that adheres to enterocyte brush borders
options.explanation: Giardia is a non-invasive luminal protozoan with teardrop-shaped binucleated trophozoites that coat the villi without invading macrophages or staining PAS-positive.

options.text: Cryptosporidium hominis, an intracellular apicomplexan protozoan causing watery secretory diarrhea
options.explanation: Cryptosporidium lines the apical brush border of enterocytes as tiny basophilic spheres (acid-fast positive); it does not pack lamina propria macrophages with PAS-positive material.

options.text: Entamoeba histolytica, an invasive amoebic protozoan that phagocytoses host erythrocytes
options.explanation: Entamoeba histolytica causes flask-shaped intestinal ulcers and amoebic liver abscesses; trophozoites ingest red blood cells (erythrophagocytosis), not PAS-positive granules in macrophages.

subject: Pathology
topic: Autoimmune Atrophic Gastritis Parietal Cell H+/K+-ATPase Destruction
stem: A 58-year-old woman with a history of Hashimoto thyroiditis and vitiligo presents to the clinic complaining of worsening fatigue, tingling in her feet, and lightheadedness. Complete blood count demonstrates severe macrocytic anemia: hemoglobin 7.4 g/dL, MCV 116 fL, and normal white blood cell and platelet counts. Serum vitamin B12 concentration is undetectable (< 50 pg/mL), and red blood cell folate is normal. Serum antiparietal cell and anti-intrinsic factor antibodies are strongly positive. Upper endoscopy reveals marked thinning and flattening of the mucosal rugal folds restricted strictly to the gastric fundus and body, with complete endoscopic sparing of the gastric antrum and pylorus. Fasting gastric fluid analysis demonstrates a pH of 7.2 (profound achlorhydria). Fasting serum gastrin concentration is markedly elevated at 1,650 pg/mL (normal: < 100 pg/mL). Multiple endoscopic mucosal biopsies of the gastric body reveal glandular atrophy, loss of specialized oxyntic parietal and chief cells, chronic lymphocytic and plasma cell infiltration, and extensive intestinal metaplasia with goblet cells. In this patient, the continuous, unregulated trophic stimulation driven by severe hypergastrinemia places her at high risk for developing which of the following secondary neoplastic processes?

options.text: Mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT) B-cell lymphoma driven by persistent antigen-dependent proliferation
options.explanation: Gastric MALT lymphoma is strongly associated with chronic Helicobacter pylori infection (Type B antral-predominant gastritis), not autoimmune atrophic gastritis, and regresses with antibiotic eradication of H. pylori.

options.text: Gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST) harboring somatic gain-of-function c-Kit proto-oncogene mutations
options.explanation: GIST arises from the interstitial cells of Cajal in the muscularis propria driven by c-Kit or PDGFRA mutations, unrelated to hypergastrinemia or achlorhydria.

options.text: Diffuse enterochromaffin-like (ECL) cell hyperplasia progressing to gastric neuroendocrine (carcinoid) tumors
options.explanation: The patient has autoimmune metaplastic atrophic gastritis (Type A gastritis), an organ-specific autoimmune disorder characterized by CD4+ T-cell-mediated destruction of gastric parietal cells and autoantibodies directed against the parietal cell H+/K+-ATPase and intrinsic factor. Parietal cells are concentrated exclusively in the oxyntic mucosa of the gastric fundus and body; the antrum is spared. Progressive parietal cell loss produces two critical pathophysiological consequences: (1) Loss of intrinsic factor causes failure of cobalamin absorption in the terminal ileum, leading to pernicious anemia (megaloblastic anemia and subacute combined degeneration); and (2) Loss of parietal cell hydrochloric acid secretion causes persistent achlorhydria (gastric fluid pH > 6.0). Under normal physiology, luminal acid acts via antral D cells (secreting somatostatin) to tonically inhibit gastrin release from antral G cells. In achlorhydria, this negative feedback loop is completely broken, triggering massive compensatory G-cell hyperplasia and extreme hypergastrinemia (often > 1,000 pg/mL). Gastrin exerts a potent trophic, mitogenic effect on enterochromaffin-like (ECL) cells in the gastric body mucosa, inducing diffuse ECL cell hyperplasia, microcarcinoids, and eventual multifocal Type 1 gastric neuroendocrine (carcinoid) tumors. In addition, chronic atrophic gastritis with intestinal metaplasia carries a 3-fold increased risk of gastric adenocarcinoma.

options.text: Gastric diffuse-type signet-ring cell adenocarcinoma driven by germline CDH1 (E-cadherin) mutations
options.explanation: Hereditary diffuse gastric cancer is caused by germline CDH1 (E-cadherin) mutations (linitis plastica), whereas autoimmune gastritis predisposes to intestinal-type adenocarcinoma.

options.text: Squamous cell carcinoma of the gastroesophageal junction secondary to persistent gastroesophageal acid reflux
options.explanation: Acid reflux causes Barrett esophagus and adenocarcinoma, not squamous carcinoma; furthermore, patients with autoimmune gastritis have zero acid secretion (achlorhydria).

subject: Anatomy
topic: Hirschsprung Disease Neural Crest Craniocaudal Migration Failure
stem: A 3-day-old male neonate born at 39 weeks gestation to a 22-year-old primigravida has failed to pass meconium since birth. Over the past 24 hours, he has developed progressive abdominal distension, poor feeding, and repeated episodes of bilious vomiting. Physical examination reveals an irritable, distended neonate with visible peristaltic waves across the anterior abdominal wall. Digital rectal examination reveals a narrow, tight rectal vault; upon withdrawal of the examiner’s gloved finger, there is an immediate, forceful, explosive expulsion of foul-smelling liquid stool and flatus ("squirt sign" or "blast sign"), with temporary relief of abdominal distension. A contrast enema reveals a narrow, spastic, caliber-reduced rectosigmoid segment with a sharp transition zone leading into a massively dilated proximal descending colon (megacolon). The infant undergoes a transanal rectal suction mucosal and submucosal biopsy taken 2 cm proximal to the pectinate line. Microscopic examination of the submucosa and muscularis mucosae demonstrates a complete absence of ganglion cells, accompanied by prominent hypertrophy of non-myelinated acetylcholinesterase-positive nerve trunks. This congenital malformation is caused by the premature arrest of which of the following embryonic developmental processes?

options.text: Incomplete lateral folding of the embryonic disc resulting in failure of abdominal wall closure
options.explanation: Failure of lateral body wall folds to fuse causes gastroschisis or omphalocele, abdominal wall defects presenting with eviscerated bowel, not colonic aganglionosis.

options.text: Failure of physiological recanalization of the intestinal lumen following solid-stage epithelial proliferation
options.explanation: Failure of luminal recanalization during weeks 8–10 causes duodenal atresia (associated with Down syndrome, presenting with "double-bubble" sign on radiograph), not megacolon.

options.text: Abnormal counterclockwise 270-degree rotation of the midgut loop around the superior mesenteric artery
options.explanation: Midgut malrotation causes volvulus and Ladd band compression of the duodenum, presenting with midgut strangulation and vomiting, not absence of rectal ganglion cells.

options.text: Craniocaudal migration of vagal neural crest-derived neuroblasts into the distal hindgut wall
options.explanation: The infant has Hirschsprung disease (congenital aganglionic megacolon), a developmental disorder characterized by functional bowel obstruction. During embryonic development (weeks 5–12), neuroblasts originating from the vagal neural crest enter the primitive foregut and migrate in a strict craniocaudal direction along the entire length of the developing alimentary canal, eventually settling in the hindgut to form the enteric nervous system. Signaling through the RET proto-oncogene (a receptor tyrosine kinase on chromosome 10q11) and its ligand GDNF (glial cell line-derived neurotrophic factor), along with the endothelin-B receptor (EDNRB) pathway, is required to guide and sustain this neural crest migration. Inactivating mutations in RET (present in ~50% of familial cases) or Down syndrome impair this migration. Because migration proceeds craniocaudally, the distal rectum is ALWAYS affected (extending proximally for variable distances: short-segment in 80%, long-segment in 20%). The aganglionic bowel segment completely lacks parasympathetic ganglion cells in both the myenteric (Auerbach) plexus and submucosal (Meissner) plexus. Without inhibitory enteric motor neurons (which release NO and VIP to induce smooth muscle relaxation), the aganglionic distal segment remains permanently contracted, producing functional bowel obstruction, failure to pass meconium, and secondary proximal megacolon.

options.text: Failure of the embryonic vitelline (omphalomesenteric) duct to completely obliterate
options.explanation: Persistence of the vitelline duct produces a Meckel diverticulum (painless lower GI bleeding in toddlers) or vitelline fistula, which contains normal ganglion cells.

subject: Immunology
topic: Chronic Granulomatous Disease DHR Flow Cytometry Defect
stem: A 4-year-old boy is brought to the pediatric hospital with high fevers, productive cough, and a painful, draining skin abscess in his right axilla. Over the past 3 years, he has required hospitalization for Serratia marcescens osteomyelitis, recurrent subcutaneous Staphylococcus aureus abscesses, and invasive pulmonary aspergillosis. Physical examination reveals an acutely ill child with a 4-cm fluctuant, tender, erythematous right axillary mass and generalized cervical lymphadenopathy. A chest radiograph demonstrates a dense, cavitary consolidation in the left upper lobe with adjacent mediastinal lymphadenopathy. Aspiration of the axillary abscess yields purulent fluid that grows Burkholderia cepacia complex. Flow cytometric analysis of the patient’s peripheral blood neutrophils is performed following in vitro stimulation with phorbol myristate acetate (PMA). While stimulated neutrophils from a healthy control demonstrate a 100-fold increase in green fluorescence intensity following the oxidation of non-fluorescent dihydrorhodamine-123 (DHR) into fluorescent rhodamine, the patient’s neutrophils demonstrate a complete absence of rhodamine fluorescence shift (flat curve). In addition, an older nitroblue tetrazolium (NBT) dye reduction slide test reveals that 0% of the patient’s neutrophils reduce yellow NBT into dark blue formazan granules. The molecular defect responsible for this child’s recurrent infections involves which of the following multi-component enzymatic systems?

options.text: Myeloperoxidase within azurophilic granules failing to convert hydrogen peroxide into hypochlorous acid
options.explanation: Myeloperoxidase (MPO) deficiency causes normal DHR and NBT tests because NADPH oxidase still produces abundant superoxide and H2O2; patients are usually asymptomatic except for mild Candida infections.

options.text: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) in the cytosol depleting cellular NADPH reducing equivalents
options.explanation: Severe G6PD deficiency can impair the respiratory burst, but primary G6PD deficiency presents with acute episodic hemolytic anemia, bite cells, and Heinz bodies.

options.text: Lysosomal trafficking regulator (LYST) preventing microtubule-mediated phagolysosomal fusion
options.explanation: LYST mutations cause Chédiak-Higashi syndrome (partial albinism, neuropathy, giant azurophilic granules), which produces normal superoxide generation.

options.text: Interleukin-12 receptor beta-1 subunit preventing Th1 cell differentiation and interferon-gamma release
options.explanation: IL-12R deficiency causes Mendelian susceptibility to mycobacterial disease (disseminated BCG or nontuberculous mycobacteria), with normal neutrophil oxidative burst assays.

options.text: The multi-subunit membrane-bound NADPH oxidase complex failing to transfer electrons from NADPH to molecular oxygen
options.explanation: The patient has Chronic Granulomatous Disease (CGD), a primary immunodeficiency characterized by defective phagocytic killing of ingested microorganisms. In ~70% of cases, CGD is X-linked recessive, caused by mutations in the CYBB gene encoding gp91phox (the catalytic beta-subunit of the cytochrome b558 heterodimer in the NADPH oxidase complex); autosomal recessive forms involve p47phox, p67phox, or p22phox. Under normal physiology, phagocytosis stimulates the assembly of cytosolic components with membrane-bound cytochrome b558 to form the active NADPH oxidase complex on phagolysosomal membranes. NADPH oxidase catalyzes the respiratory (oxidative) burst: it transfers electrons from NADPH to molecular oxygen (O2) to generate superoxide anions (O2*-). Superoxide is then dismutated to hydrogen peroxide (H2O2), which myeloperoxidase (MPO) uses to generate hypochlorous acid (HOCl / bleach), destroying phagocytosed microbes. stem: A 15-month-old boy is admitted to the pediatric intensive care unit with high fevers, jaundice, abdominal distension, and respiratory distress. He was delivered at term to consanguineous parents. Physical examination reveals an acutely ill toddler with striking silvery-gray, metallic hair, pale skin compared to his parents, and pale gray irides. Abdominal palpation reveals massive hepatosplenomegaly, and lymphadenopathy is present. Laboratory evaluation demonstrates life-threatening hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH): pancytopenia (hemoglobin 6.4 g/dL, absolute neutrophil count 380/microL, platelet count 28,000/microL), marked hyperferritinemia (ferritin 18,500 ng/mL), hypertriglyceridemia (triglycerides 640 mg/dL), and hypofibrinogenemia (fibrinogen 65 mg/dL). Natural killer (NK) cell and cytotoxic T-cell degranulation assays demonstrate absent lytic granule exocytosis. Peripheral blood smear examination demonstrates normal-sized, morphologically conventional cytoplasmic granules within all circulating neutrophils and monocytes, with a complete absence of giant azurophilic granules. Light microscopic examination of the patient’s hair shafts reveals prominent, irregular, large aggregates and clumps of melanin pigment unevenly distributed along the central hair medullary shaft. Genetic sequencing confirms Griscelli syndrome type 2. This disorder is caused by a genetic defect in which of the following molecular mechanisms?

options.text: A small Rab-family GTPase (Rab27a) coordinating actin-dependent transport and exocytosis of lytic granules and melanosomes
options.explanation: The patient has Griscelli syndrome type 2 (GS2), a rare autosomal recessive immunodeficiency characterized by partial oculocutaneous albinism (silvery-metallic hair and pale skin), defective natural killer (NK) cell / cytotoxic T-lymphocyte (CTL) cytotoxicity, and fatal accelerated hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH). GS2 is caused by mutations in the RAB27A gene on chromosome 15q21, which encodes Rab27a, a small monomeric Ras-related GTPase. Rab27a forms a tripartite complex with melanophilin (MLPH) and myosin Va (MYO5A) that tethers melanosomes to the peripheral actin cytoskeleton in melanocytes, allowing melanosomes to be transferred to keratinocytes; in cytotoxic T cells and NK cells, Rab27a coordinates the docking and exocytic fusion of perforin- and granzyme-containing lytic granules with the plasma membrane. Defective Rab27a paralyzes cytotoxic lymphocyte killing and melanosome secretion. Crucially, Griscelli syndrome is differentiated from Chédiak-Higashi syndrome (LYST mutation) by peripheral blood smear cytology: Chédiak-Higashi displays pathognomonic GIANT azurophilic lysosomal granules in leukocytes, whereas Griscelli syndrome displays COMPLETELY NORMAL, conventional-sized granules. options.explanation: LYST mutations cause Chédiak-Higashi syndrome, which is definitively ruled out by the absence of giant azurophilic granules on the peripheral blood smear.

options.explanation: ABCD1 mutations cause X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy, presenting with behavioral changes, white matter demyelination, and primary adrenal failure, not silvery hair or HLH.

options.text: A motor protein dynein heavy chain coordinating retrograde axonal transport along microtubules
options.explanation: Dynein mutations cause primary ciliary dyskinesia or hereditary motor neuropathies, not cutaneous hypopigmentation or cytotoxic granule defects.

options.explanation: ATP7B mutations cause Wilson disease (Kayser-Fleischer rings, basal ganglia degeneration, cirrhosis), unrelated to Rab GTPases or albinism.

subject: Immunology
topic: APECED Syndrome AIRE Gene Negative Selection Defect
stem: A 9-year-old girl is brought to the pediatric endocrinology clinic for evaluation of painful muscle spasms in her hands and chronic recurrent oral thrush. Since infancy, she has suffered severe, persistent Candida albicans infections involving her oral mucosa, tongue, and fingernails that have been refractory to multiple courses of topical nystatin. Over the past 6 months, she has experienced muscle cramps, numbness around her lips, and progressive generalized fatigue. Physical examination reveals white, curdy plaques over the buccal mucosa with cracked, thickened, dystrophic fingernails. Tapping over the facial nerve anterior to the ear elicits brisk twitching of the ipsilateral orbicularis oris and alae nasi (positive Chvostek sign). Examination of her teeth reveals marked pitting and horizontal grooving of the dental enamel (enamel hypoplasia). Laboratory evaluation reveals: serum calcium 6.8 mg/dL (markedly low; normal: 8.5–10.5 mg/dL), serum phosphorus 6.4 mg/dL (elevated; normal: 2.5–4.5 mg/dL), intact parathyroid hormone (iPTH) undetectable (< 5 pg/mL), morning serum cortisol 3.2 microg/dL (low; normal: 5–25 microg/dL), and plasma ACTH 320 pg/mL (elevated; normal: 10–60 pg/mL). High titers of neutralizing autoantibodies against interleukin-17A and interleukin-22 are present in serum. Genetic analysis confirms an inactivating mutation in the AIRE gene on chromosome 21q22. The protein encoded by this mutated gene normally coordinates which of the following essential immunological processes?

options.text: Transcription factor induction of CD4+CD25+ regulatory T-cell lineage commitment via FoxP3
options.explanation: FoxP3 coordinates regulatory T-cell differentiation; mutations cause IPEX syndrome (neonatal diabetes, enteropathy, eczema), not AIRE-dependent APS-1.

options.text: Ectopic transcription of tissue-restricted peripheral self-antigens in medullary thymic epithelial cells to mediate negative selection of developing T cells
options.explanation: The patient has Autoimmune Polyendocrinopathy-Candidiasis-Ectodermal Dystrophy (APECED), also known as Autoimmune Polyglandular Syndrome Type 1 (APS-1). APS-1 is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by inactivating mutations in the AIRE (Autoimmune Regulator) gene on chromosome 21q22.3. The AIRE protein is a master transcriptional regulator expressed predominantly in the nuclei of medullary thymic epithelial cells (mTECs). AIRE interacts with chromatin and RNA polymerase II to drive "promiscuous" or ectopic expression of thousands of peripheral, tissue-restricted self-antigens (such as insulin, parathyroid calcium-sensing receptor, thyroid peroxidase, and adrenal 21-hydroxylase) within the thymic microenvironment. During the process of CENTRAL TOLERANCE, developing single-positive (CD4+ or CD8+) thymocytes whose T-cell receptors (TCRs) bind with high avidity to these self-antigens presented on MHC molecules receive death signals and undergo apoptosis (negative selection / clonal deletion). When AIRE is non-functional, autoreactive T-cell clones fail to be eliminated, escaping into the peripheral circulation where they orchestrate autoimmune destruction of multiple endocrine organs. APS-1 is characterized by the classic triad of: (1) Chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis (CMC, appearing in early infancy, driven by high-titer autoantibodies against Th17 cytokines IL-17A, IL-17F, and IL-22); (2) Autoimmune hypoparathyroidism (appearing in childhood, causing hypocalcemia and tetany); and (3) Primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease, appearing in adolescence). Ectodermal dystrophy (dental enamel hypoplasia, nail dystrophy, vitiligo) is an associated hallmark.

options.text: Fas-ligand (CD95L) mediated activation-induced cell death of mature peripheral autoreactive B cells
options.explanation: Fas/FasL mutations impair peripheral apoptosis and cause Autoimmune Lymphoproliferative Syndrome (ALPS), characterized by non-malignant lymphadenopathy and double-negative T cells.

options.text: Somatic recombination of immunoglobulin V(D)J gene segments catalyzed by RAG-1 and RAG-2
options.explanation: RAG-1/RAG-2 endonucleases mediate V(D)J recombination; mutations cause T- B- SCID or Omenn syndrome, not autoimmune endocrinopathies.

options.text: Assembly of the major histocompatibility complex class I peptide-loading complex via TAP-1
options.explanation: TAP transporter defects cause Bare Lymphocyte Syndrome Type I (MHC class I deficiency), characterized by recurrent sinopulmonary and skin bacterial infections.

subject: Immunology
topic: IPEX Syndrome FOXP3 Regulatory T-Cell Deficiency
stem: A 3-week-old male infant is admitted to the pediatric intensive care unit with severe, life-threatening watery diarrhea (12–15 bowel movements daily), intractable vomiting, extreme dehydration, and severe failure to thrive. He was born at term following an uncomplicated pregnancy. Over the past week, he has also developed widespread, severe, peeling eczematous erythroderma over his face, trunk, and diaper area. Physical examination reveals an emaciated, tachypneic infant with sunken fontanelles, generalized lymphadenopathy, and marked abdominal distension. Initial laboratory evaluation reveals: plasma glucose 480 mg/dL, arterial pH 7.18, serum bicarbonate 10 mEq/L, and elevated anion gap (24 mEq/L) with large serum and urinary ketones, confirming diabetic ketoacidosis in a 3-week-old infant. Complete blood count reveals Coombs-positive autoimmune hemolytic anemia (hemoglobin 7.2 g/dL) and marked eosinophilia. Serum IgE concentration is markedly elevated at 2,400 IU/mL. Upper and lower endoscopy reveals diffuse mucosal erythema with complete subtotal villous blunting and dense mononuclear lymphocytic infiltration throughout the small bowel and colon. Flow cytometry reveals normal numbers of CD4+ and CD8+ T cells, but functional assays demonstrate a complete absence of peripheral CD4+CD25+ regulatory T-cell suppressor activity. This fatal infant syndrome is caused by a genetic mutation in a master transcription factor encoded on the X chromosome that is essential for the development of which of the following immune cell populations?

options.text: CD19+ CD20+ mature naive B lymphocytes undergoing germinal center affinity maturation
options.explanation: B-cell development is governed by Pax5 and Bruton tyrosine kinase (BTK); BTK mutations cause X-linked agammaglobulinemia, characterized by recurrent bacterial infections, not neonatal diabetes or IPEX.

options.text: CD56+ CD16+ natural killer (NK) cells mediating antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity
options.explanation: NK-cell development requires the common gamma chain (IL-15 receptor) and T-bet; defects cause susceptibility to viral infections, not IPEX syndrome.

options.text: CD4+ CD25+ regulatory T lymphocytes (Tregs) that maintain peripheral immune tolerance and suppress autoreactive effector T cells
options.explanation: The infant has IPEX syndrome (Immune dysregulation, Polyendocrinopathy, Enteropathy, X-linked), a rare, fatal congenital disorder of immune tolerance caused by hemizygous loss-of-function mutations in the FOXP3 gene on chromosome Xp11.23. The FOXP3 gene encodes Forkhead Box P3, an indispensable transcription factor that specifies the differentiation, functional maturation, and suppressive program of natural and induced CD4+ CD25+ regulatory T cells (Tregs). Under normal physiology, regulatory T cells express high levels of the IL-2 receptor alpha chain (CD25), CTLA-4, and FoxP3. Tregs enforce PERIPHERAL TOLERANCE by actively suppressing self-reactive effector T cells (Th1, Th2, Th17) that have escaped thymic negative selection. Tregs suppress autoreactivity through multiple mechanisms: (1) direct cell-to-cell contact via CTLA-4 (downregulating CD80/CD86 on APCs); (2) secretion of immunosuppressive cytokines (IL-10, TGF-beta, and IL-35); (3) consumption of local IL-2 (starving effector T cells); and (4) pericellular adenosine generation via CD39 and CD73. In the absence of functional FoxP3, Tregs fail to develop or function. Unrestrained autoreactive T cells mount catastrophic attacks against self-antigens, producing the classic IPEX tetrad: (1) Intractable autoimmune enteropathy with villous atrophy and profuse watery diarrhea; (2) Early neonatal-onset autoimmune type 1 diabetes mellitus (within the first months of life); (3) Severe atopic dermatitis/eczema with hyper-IgE and eosinophilia; and (4) Autoimmune cytopenias and thyroiditis. Definitive cure requires allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation.

options.text: CD1a+ Langerhans cells presenting epidermal antigens in regional lymph nodes
options.explanation: Langerhans cell histiocytosis involves neoplastic proliferation of CD1a+/Langerin+ dendritic cells with Birbeck granules, driven by BRAF V600E mutations.

options.text: CD8+ cytotoxic T lymphocytes mediating perforin-dependent apoptosis of viral targets
options.explanation: CD8+ T-cell development requires MHC class I and Runx3; in IPEX, CD8+ T cells are present and hyperactive due to lack of Treg suppression.

subject: Immunology
topic: Hereditary Angioedema C1 Inhibitor Deficiency Pathophysiology
stem: A 22-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with severe, non-pruritic swelling of her lips, tongue, and face that began 6 hours after undergoing an uncomplicated wisdom tooth extraction. She also reports severe, crampy, diffuse abdominal pain and nausea. Over the past 4 years, she has experienced three similar episodes of painless, non-pitting swelling involving her hands and feet following minor physical trauma or emotional stress, each lasting 2 to 3 days before resolving spontaneously. Notably, she has never experienced urticaria (hives) or itching during these episodes. Physical examination reveals marked, asymmetric, painless edema of the upper and lower lips, tongue, and periorbital tissues, without erythema, warmth, or wheals. Stridor is not audible, but her voice is breathy. In the emergency department, she is administered intramuscular epinephrine, intravenous diphenhydramine, and intravenous methylprednisolone; however, 2 hours later, her facial swelling and abdominal pain remain completely unchanged. Abdominal ultrasonography reveals transient thickening and edema of the jejunal wall with free fluid in the pelvis. Laboratory evaluation demonstrates: serum complement C4 profoundly decreased at 4 mg/dL (normal: 16–47 mg/dL), serum complement C1q normal, and serum complement C3 normal. The primary vasoactive mediator directly driving this patient’s tissue edema and vascular hyperpermeability is produced through which of the following enzymatic pathways?

options.text: Degranulation of mucosal mast cells releasing preformed histamine and newly synthesized leukotriene C4
options.explanation: Mast cell degranulation causes allergic angioedema (Type I hypersensitivity), which is accompanied by intense pruritus and urticaria (hives) and responds briskly to epinephrine and antihistamines.

options.text: Platelet activation and cyclooxygenase-1 synthesis of thromboxane A2 driving arteriolar spasm
options.explanation: Thromboxane A2 causes vasoconstriction and platelet aggregation, the opposite of the intense vasodilation and edema in angioedema.

options.text: Alternative complement pathway activation generating massive amounts of the membrane attack complex (C5b-9)
options.explanation: C5b-9 mediates cell lysis; in HAE, swelling is mediated by bradykinin, not membrane attack complex formation.

options.text: Unchecked activation of plasma kallikrein cleaving high-molecular-weight kininogen into bradykinin
options.explanation: The patient has hereditary angioedema (HAE), an autosomal dominant condition caused by quantitative deficiency (Type I, 85%) or functional dysfunction (Type II, 15%) of C1 esterase inhibitor (C1-INH), encoded by the SERPING1 gene. C1-INH is a serine protease inhibitor (serpin) that physiological regulates two vital cascades: (1) the classical complement pathway (inhibiting activated C1r and C1s proteases); and (2) the contact activation (kallikrein-kinin) cascade (inhibiting activated factor XIIa and plasma kallikrein). Under normal conditions, C1-INH keeps plasma kallikrein strictly in check. In HAE, loss of C1-INH allows activated factor XIIa and uninhibited kallikrein to cleave high-molecular-weight kininogen (HMWK), generating massive amounts of the vasoactive nonapeptide BRADYKININ. Bradykinin acts on endothelial B2 receptors, activating nitric oxide synthase and prostacyclin, producing intense arteriolar vasodilation and profound postcapillary venular hyperpermeability. Crucially, HAE is a kinin-mediated angioedema, NOT a mast cell / histamine-mediated allergic reaction: it characteristically presents WITHOUT urticaria, pruritus, or flushing, and is completely refractory to antihistamines, corticosteroids, and epinephrine. Swelling of the larynx causes fatal asphyxiation. Laboratory diagnosis is confirmed by a persistently low complement C4 level (due to uninhibited C1 cleavage of C4 and C2), with normal C1q (differentiating HAE from acquired C1-INH deficiency). Treatment involves C1-INH concentrates, icatibant (a selective bradykinin B2 receptor antagonist), or ecallantide (a kallikrein inhibitor). ACE inhibitors are strictly contraindicated because ACE normally degrades bradykinin.

options.text: Endothelial overexpression of endothelin-1 stimulating vascular smooth muscle ETA receptors

explanation: The patient has hereditary angioedema (HAE), an autosomal dominant condition caused by quantitative deficiency (Type I, 85%) or functional dysfunction (Type II, 15%) of C1 esterase inhibitor (C1-INH), encoded by the SERPING1 gene. topic: Pemphigus Vulgaris vs Bullous Pemphigoid Desmosome Pathology
stem: A 48-year-old Jewish woman presents to the dermatology clinic with painful sores in her mouth that have persisted for 4 months, making eating solid foods excruciating. Over the past 3 weeks, she has developed multiple blisters on her scalp, face, chest, and back. Physical examination reveals extensive, painful, irregular erosions and ulcerations covering the buccal mucosa, hard palate, and gingiva. Dermatological examination of the trunk reveals scattered, thin-walled, flaccid bullae on normal-appearing skin, along with numerous large, weeping, denuded erosions with crusting where blisters have ruptured. When the physician applies firm lateral sliding pressure with a thumb to normal-appearing skin adjacent to an erosion, the superficial epidermis easily slips and detaches from the underlying dermis, producing a new blister (positive Nikolsky sign). A punch biopsy of an intact lesion and adjacent perilesional skin is performed. Microscopic examination demonstrates an intraepidermal blister located immediately above the basal cell layer (suprabasal acantholysis); the separated keratinocytes appear rounded and detached (acantholytic cells), while a single layer of intact basal keratinocytes remains firmly attached to the underlying dermis, resembling a "row of tombstones." Direct immunofluorescence microscopy of perilesional epidermis reveals a delicate, reticular, "net-like" or "fishnet" pattern of IgG and complement C3 deposition throughout the intercellular spaces of the stratum spinosum. The autoantibodies responsible for this blistering disease target which of the following cellular adhesion structures?

options.text: Hemidesmosomal transmembrane collagenous glycoproteins (BP180 and BP230) anchoring basal cells to the lamina lucida
options.explanation: Autoantibodies targeting hemidesmosomes (BP180 / type XVII collagen and BP230) cause Bullous Pemphigoid, characterized by deep, TENSE subepidermal bullae, negative Nikolsky sign, linear basement membrane IgG deposition, and rare oral involvement.

options.text: Type VII collagen anchoring fibrils linking the lamina densa to interstitial dermal type I collagen
options.explanation: Type VII collagen autoantibodies cause Epidermolysis Bullosa Acquisita (EBA), producing subepidermal mechanobullous blisters over extensor trauma sites, not flaccid intraepidermal suprabasal blisters.

options.text: Zonula occludens (tight junction) transmembrane proteins claudin and occludin
options.explanation: Tight junctions form the apical paracellular barrier in simple epithelia and stratum granulosum; they are not the target in pemphigus vulgaris.

options.text: Connexin-43 hexameric hemichannels forming intercellular gap junctions
options.explanation: Gap junctions mediate electrical and metabolic intercellular communication (connexins); mutations cause palmoplantar keratoderma and deafness, not pemphigus acantholysis.

options.text: Desmosomal cadherin glycoproteins (desmoglein-3 and desmoglein-1) connecting adjacent spinous keratinocytes
options.explanation: The patient has pemphigus vulgaris (PV), a life-threatening autoimmune intraepidermal blistering dermatosis. PV is caused by pathogenic IgG autoantibodies (primarily IgG4) directed against desmoglein-3 (expressed throughout mucosal stratified squamous epithelium and lower epidermis) and desmoglein-1 (expressed in upper epidermis). Desmogleins are calcium-dependent transmembrane cadherin cell-adhesion glycoproteins that form the core of DESMOSOMES (maculae adherentes), which provide mechanical intercellular anchoring between adjacent keratinocytes in the stratum spinosum. Autoantibody binding induces steric hindrance and activates intracellular signaling cascades (including p38 MAPK) that cause endocytosis and degradation of desmosomes. Disruption of intercellular bridges causes loss of keratinocyte cohesion, a process termed ACANTHOLYSIS. The resulting blisters are thin-walled, intraepidermal (suprabasal), and FLACCID; they rupture exceptionally easily, leaving painful, weeping, denuded erosions. Nikolsky sign and Asboe-Hansen sign (lateral blister extension upon pressure) are positive. Because basal keratinocytes remain attached to the basement membrane via intact hemidesmosomes, histology reveals a diagnostic "row of tombstones." Direct immunofluorescence reveals a pathognomonic "fishnet" or "chicken-wire" pattern of intercellular IgG/C3. Oral mucosal erosions occur in >90% of patients and precede skin lesions.

topic: Dermatitis Herpetiformis Epidermal Transglutaminase-3 IgA Deposition
stem: A 28-year-old man presents to the dermatology clinic with an excruciatingly itchy, burning skin rash over his elbows, knees, and buttocks that has persisted for 6 months. He states that the itch is unremitting and that scratching leads to bleeding and crusting. He reports no abdominal pain, diarrhea, or weight loss. Physical examination reveals an alert young man with symmetric, clustered, excoriated, erythematous papules and tiny, tense, grouped vesicles ("herpetiform" arrangement) distributed over the extensor aspects of both elbows, both knees, the sacral region, and the upper buttocks. A punch biopsy of an intact early vesicle and perilesional skin is performed. Microscopic examination demonstrates subepidermal clefting with collections of neutrophils and nuclear dust (neutrophilic microabscesses) localized specifically within the tips of the dermal papillae, accompanied by focal vacuolar alteration of the basal cell layer. Direct immunofluorescence (DIF) microscopy of uninvolved perilesional skin demonstrates granular, clumpy deposits of Immunoglobulin A (IgA) concentrated exclusively in the tips of the dermal papillae along the dermoepidermal junction. Oral dapsone therapy is initiated, resulting in dramatic cessation of itching and healing of skin lesions within 48 hours. The cutaneous pathology in this patient is driven by immune cross-reactivity with an antigen primarily expressed in which of the following extracutaneous tissues?

options.text: Small intestinal mucosa, sharing homology between epidermal transglutaminase (tTG-3) and intestinal tissue transglutaminase (tTG-2)
options.explanation: The patient has dermatitis herpetiformis (DH), an intensely pruritic, autoimmune subepidermal blistering disease that represents the specific cutaneous manifestation of celiac disease (gluten-sensitive enteropathy). Greater than 90% to 100% of patients with DH have underlying histological evidence of celiac disease on duodenal biopsy (villous blunting, crypt hyperplasia), although the majority are entirely asymptomatic gastrointestinally. In the gut, dietary gluten stimulates production of mucosal IgA directed against intestinal tissue transglutaminase (tTG-2). These antibodies cross-react with high affinity against epidermal transglutaminase (eTG / tTG-3), an enzyme involved in maintaining the cornified epidermal envelope. High-affinity IgA-eTG3 immune complexes circulate in the bloodstream and deposit selectively in a GRANULAR pattern within the fibrillin microfibrils in the tips of the dermal papillae of the skin. Deposited IgA immune complexes activate complement via the alternative pathway, generating C5a, which recruits neutrophils into the papillary tips. Neutrophil release of elastase and collagenase digests the basement membrane, producing microscopic subepidermal blisters and intense pruritus. Treatment: oral dapsone provides rapid clinical relief within 24 to 48 hours by suppressing neutrophil chemotaxis, myeloperoxidase activity, and integrin adhesion; however, a strict, lifelong gluten-free diet is the only definitive curative therapy, as it clears the circulating IgA-tTG complexes over 1 to 2 years.

options.text: Synovial joint capsule, targeting citrullinated filaggrin and vimentin peptides
options.explanation: Anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (anti-CCP) antibodies are specific for rheumatoid arthritis, presenting with erosive symmetric polyarthritis, not dermal papillae IgA deposition.

options.text: Renal glomerular and pulmonary alveolar basement membrane type IV collagen alpha-3 chains
options.explanation: Anti-GBM antibodies targeting the alpha-3 chain of type IV collagen cause Goodpasture disease, presenting with rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis and pulmonary hemorrhage.

options.text: Thyroid follicular cell apical membranes expressing thyroid peroxidase and thyroglobulin
options.explanation: Anti-TPO antibodies cause Hashimoto thyroiditis; while Hashimoto may co-occur with celiac disease, it does not generate the IgA complexes of dermatitis herpetiformis.

options.text: Myelin basic protein and proteolipid protein in central nervous system oligodendrocytes
options.explanation: Autoimmune myelin attack occurs in Multiple Sclerosis, presenting with relapsing central neurological deficits, unrelated to cutaneous vesicular lesions.

subject: Pathology
topic: Erythema Multiforme CD8 T-Cell Keratinocyte Apoptosis Pathology
stem: A 24-year-old previously healthy man presents to the urgent care clinic with an acute eruption of multiple itchy spots on his hands, arms, and legs that appeared 48 hours ago. He reports that 10 days ago, he developed a painful cluster of small blisters on the vermilion border of his lower lip ("cold sore") that crusted and healed completely. Physical examination reveals an alert, afebrile man with normal vital signs. Dermatological examination reveals multiple symmetric, discrete, round, sharply demarcated erythematous papules and plaques clustered over the dorsum of both hands, palms, extensor forearms, and soles of both feet. Many lesions display a striking, pathognomonic concentric morphology featuring three distinct zones: a central dark-red or dusky purpuric center, surrounded by an elevated, pale edematous intermediate zone, bordered by a sharp, outer erythematous ring (classic "target" or "iris" lesions). Examination of the oral cavity reveals two minor superficial erosions on the lower labial mucosa without extensive sloughing; ocular and genital mucous membranes are completely uninvolved. A punch biopsy of a targetoid lesion demonstrates vacuolar degeneration of the basal cell layer, subepidermal edema, a dense superficial perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate along the dermoepidermal junction, and individual necrotic/apoptotic keratinocytes surrounded by cytotoxic lymphocytes (satellite cell necrosis). Which of the following immunopathological mechanisms is responsible for the cutaneous target lesions in this patient?

options.text: Type III immune complex vasculitis with intense leukocytoclastic neutrophilic postcapillary venular necrosis
options.explanation: Type III immune complex leukocytoclastic vasculitis causes palpable purpura (seen in Henoch-Schönlein purpura or cryoglobulinemia), lacking concentric targetoid zones or satellite cell apoptosis.

options.text: Cell-mediated hypersensitivity reaction wherein CD8+ cytotoxic T lymphocytes target viral antigen-bearing epidermal keratinocytes
options.explanation: The patient has erythema multiforme (EM minor), an acute, self-limiting type IV (cell-mediated) hypersensitivity reaction of the skin and mucous membranes. The overwhelming majority of EM cases (> 70% to 90%) are triggered by preceding infection with Herpes Simplex Virus (most commonly HSV-1 labial herpes, occurring 1 to 2 weeks prior to the rash). Other infectious triggers include Mycoplasma pneumoniae (which often causes severe mucosal involvement, known as MIRM), fungal infections, and certain medications. The immunopathogenesis of HSV-associated EM involves: (1) During the primary or recurrent viral flare, circulating CD34+ cutaneous Langerhans cell precursors phagocytose HSV DNA and transport viral DNA fragments (specifically the viral DNA polymerase gene pol) to distant epidermal sites; (2) The viral gene is expressed in basal and spinous keratinocytes; (3) Host HSV-specific CD8+ cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs) are recruited to the epidermis, where they recognize viral antigens on keratinocyte MHC class I molecules; and (4) Activated CTLs release interferon-gamma, perforin, and granzyme B, triggering widespread keratinocyte apoptosis and vacuolar interface dermatitis (satellite cell necrosis). The clinical hallmark is the classic TARGET or IRIS lesion with three distinct concentric zones: central dusky necrosis, intermediate pale edema, and outer erythematous flare, located characteristically on acral surfaces (palms, soles, extensor forearms).

options.text: Type II autoantibody-mediated complement activation against desmosomal adhesion glycoproteins
options.explanation: Autoantibodies against desmoglein cause pemphigus vulgaris, presenting with flaccid bullae and a positive Nikolsky sign without target lesions.

options.text: IgE-mediated immediate mast cell degranulation with dermal histamine and leukotriene release
options.explanation: Type I hypersensitivity causes urticaria (hives), which are transient, intensely pruritic, edematous wheals that migrate and resolve within 24 hours, lacking necrotic centers.

options.text: Exotoxin-mediated cleavage of desmoglein-1 in the superficial stratum granulosum
options.explanation: Staphylococcal exfoliative toxin cleaves desmoglein-1 in Staphylococcal Scalded Skin Syndrome (SSSS), presenting with diffuse superficial skin peeling in neonates, without target lesions.

subject: Pathology
topic: Cutaneous Melanoma Breslow Depth and BRAF V600E Mutation
stem: A 54-year-old fair-skinned man presents to the dermatology clinic for evaluation of a mole on his upper back that his wife noticed has changed dramatically over the past 6 months. He has a history of multiple blistering sunburns during childhood and outdoor recreation. Physical examination reveals an asymmetric, 11-mm, pigmented plaque on the left upper scapular back. The lesion exhibits irregular, scalloped borders and marked variegation in color, displaying dark brown, jet black, reddish-pink, and pale blue-white areas. A focal 3-mm elevated, nodular component is palpated near the center of the plaque. An excisional biopsy with a 2-mm margin is performed. Microscopic examination demonstrates atypical, pleomorphic, enlarged melanocytes with prominent cherry-red nucleoli arranged in nests along the dermoepidermal junction and invading upward through all layers of the epidermis in a pagetoid pattern. In the central nodular area, atypical melanocytic nests invade deeply into the reticular dermis (vertical growth phase). Immunohistochemical staining is strongly and diffusely positive for S-100, HMB-45, and Melan-A. Molecular testing confirms the presence of a somatic BRAF V600E mutation. Which of the following histopathological measurements represents the single most important independent prognostic predictor of disease-free survival and distant metastatic risk in this patient?

options.text: Clark level of invasion categorizing tumor penetration according to histological anatomical dermal tiers
options.explanation: Clark level (levels I through V based on anatomical tiers) has been superseded by Breslow depth in international AJCC staging because numerical millimeter thickness is far more reproducible and accurate.

options.text: The presence and density of tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs) surrounding the deep tumor margin
options.explanation: Tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes indicate host immune response, but Breslow thickness remains the primary determinant of staging and prognosis.

options.text: Breslow tumor thickness measured from the top of the epidermal granular layer to the deepest invasive melanoma cell
options.explanation: The patient has primary invasive cutaneous malignant melanoma, the deadliest form of skin cancer, arising from neural crest-derived melanocytes. Melanoma development typically progresses from a radial (horizontal) growth phase (where atypical melanocytes proliferate intraepidermally along the basal layer, lacking metastatic competence) to a vertical growth phase (where neoplastic cells invade downward into the underlying dermis, forming expansile tumor nodules and acquiring access to lymphatic and vascular channels). In cutaneous melanoma, the BRESLOW DEPTH (tumor thickness) is the single most powerful and reliable histopathological predictor of 5-year and 10-year survival, regional lymph node metastasis, and distant dissemination. Breslow depth is measured with an ocular micrometer from the top of the epidermal granular cell layer (or the base of an ulcer if ulcerated) to the deepest invasive tumor cell in the dermis or subcutis. (For example, lesions < 0.8 mm have a >95% 10-year survival, while lesions > 4.0 mm have a high risk of systemic metastasis and <50% survival). Ulceration and mitotic rate are secondary prognostic features. Clark level (anatomical layer invasion) has been replaced by Breslow depth in official AJCC staging. Greater than 50% of cutaneous melanomas harbor the activating BRAF V600E mutation (amenable to targeted therapy with vemurafenib/dabrafenib plus MEK inhibitors).

options.text: The degree of melanin pigmentation and cytoplasmic melanophage density in the adjacent dermis
options.explanation: Melanin pigment quantity (melanotic vs amelanotic) does not dictate metastatic potential; depth of vertical invasion is paramount.

options.text: Maximum horizontal surface diameter of the lesion measured across the epidermal plane
options.explanation: While diameter > 6 mm is part of the clinical ABCDE diagnostic criteria, surface diameter does not correlate with survival; vertical invasion depth governs metastatic risk.

stem: A 66-year-old retired construction worker presents to the dermatology clinic for evaluation of a non-healing sore on his left nasal alar rim that has slowly enlarged over the past 8 months and bleeds whenever he washes his face. Physical examination reveals an 8-mm, translucent, shiny, pearly pink nodule with prominent, branching, arborizing telangiectatic blood vessels coursing over its surface. The lesion features raised, rolled, rolled-up borders surrounding a central shallow crater with a thin, hemorrhagic crust ("rodent ulcer"). No regional cervical lymphadenopathy is palpable. A shave biopsy of the lesion is performed. Microscopic examination demonstrates atypical lobules and cords of small, uniform, dark-blue basaloid epithelial cells with high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratios extending from the basal layer of the epidermis into the upper reticular dermis. The outermost layer of cells along the periphery of each neoplastic nest is arranged in an orderly, parallel, picket fence-like alignment (peripheral palisading). Prominent clear-space retraction artifacts (clefting) are observed between the basaloid tumor nests and the surrounding loose, myxoid, fibrotic dermal stroma. Inactivating mutations in which of the following tumor suppressor genes are the primary oncogenic driver in the pathogenesis of this neoplasm?

options.text: CDKN2A, encoding the p16-INK4a cell-cycle inhibitor that arrests cells in G1 phase via CDK4/6 binding
options.explanation: CDKN2A (p16) mutations are the most common genetic cause of familial melanoma and pancreatic cancer, not the primary driver of basal cell carcinoma.

options.text: NF1, encoding neurofibromin, a GTPase-activating protein that accelerates Ras-GTP hydrolysis
options.explanation: NF1 mutations cause Neurofibromatosis Type 1 (café-au-lait spots, neurofibromas, Lisch nodules, pheochromocytoma), not basal cell carcinoma.

options.text: APC, encoding the adenomatous polyposis coli scaffold protein coordinating beta-catenin destruction
options.explanation: APC mutations drive familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP) and sporadic colorectal adenocarcinoma, not cutaneous basaloid tumors.

options.text: PTCH1, encoding the patched-1 cell-surface receptor that tonically represses smoothened (SMO) in the Sonic hedgehog pathway
options.explanation: The patient has nodular basal cell carcinoma (BCC), the most common cancer in humans worldwide. BCC occurs overwhelmingly on chronically sun-exposed skin (especially the head and neck, face, and nose) and is induced by ultraviolet radiation (UVB causing characteristic C-to-T pyrimidine dimer transitions). Clinical features include a pearly, translucent papule or nodule with arborizing telangiectasias, rolled borders, and central ulceration. BCC is locally invasive and destructive ("rodent ulcer"), but possesses virtually zero metastatic potential (< 0.05%). The histopathological hallmark consists of: (1) islands and nests of uniform basaloid cells invading the dermis; (2) peripheral palisading (columnar alignment of basaloid nuclei around the periphery of tumor nests); and (3) retraction artifact / stromal clefting (shrinkage artifact during formalin fixation producing clear spaces between tumor nests and mucinous stroma). The molecular driver of >90% of sporadic BCCs and 100% of hereditary cases (Gorlin syndrome / Nevoid Basal Cell Carcinoma syndrome) is constitutive activation of the SONIC HEDGEHOG (SHH) signaling pathway. The PTCH1 gene (on chromosome 9q22) encodes patched-1, a 12-transmembrane receptor that acts as a tumor suppressor by constitutively binding to and repressing Smoothened (SMO). Binding of the Hedgehog ligand to PTCH1 normally relieves this repression. Inactivating mutations in PTCH1 (or activating mutations in SMO) release SMO from inhibition, driving continuous nuclear translocation of GLI1 transcription factors that transcribe genes promoting cell proliferation and survival. Advanced or inoperable BCC is treated with vismodegib or sonidegib, oral small-molecule inhibitors of SMO.

options.text: VHL, encoding the von Hippel-Lindau protein that targets hypoxia-inducible factor-1alpha for degradation
options.explanation: VHL mutations cause clear cell renal cell carcinoma, hemangioblastomas, and pheochromocytomas, not cutaneous basal cell carcinomas.

topic: Winter Formula Respiratory Compensation in Metabolic Acidosis
stem:
A 28-year-old woman with a history of type 1 diabetes mellitus is brought to the emergency department by her roommate due to severe lethargy, deep sighing respirations, vomiting, and diffuse abdominal pain. She ran out of insulin 3 days ago. On physical examination, she is obtunded, dry, and breathing deeply and rapidly (Kussmaul respirations). Vital signs: blood pressure 92/58 mm Hg, heart rate 126/min, respirations 34/min, and temperature 37.1 C. Laboratory testing reveals: serum sodium 134 mEq/L, potassium 5.6 mEq/L, chloride 98 mEq/L, and bicarbonate 10 mEq/L, with a calculated anion gap of 26 mEq/L. Blood glucose is 540 mg/dL, and urine ketones are strongly positive (diabetic ketoacidosis). An arterial blood gas (ABG) drawn while breathing room air demonstrates:
- pH: 7.22
- PaCO2: 32 mm Hg
- PaO2: 96 mm Hg
- HCO3-: 10 mEq/L
Based on Winter’s formula for expected respiratory compensation in metabolic acidosis, which of the following accurately describes this patient’s complete acid-base status?

options.text: Pure, uncompensated high anion gap metabolic acidosis with zero respiratory response
options.explanation: A normal uncompensated PaCO2 would be 40 mm Hg; the patient has reduced PaCO2 to 32 mm Hg, but it is insufficient to meet full compensation (21–25 mm Hg).

options.text: High anion gap metabolic acidosis with appropriate, fully compensated respiratory response
options.explanation: Full compensation requires PaCO2 to be within 21–25 mm Hg; a PaCO2 of 32 mm Hg represents under-compensation (superimposed respiratory acidosis).

options.text: High anion gap metabolic acidosis with a concurrent primary respiratory alkalosis
options.explanation: Concurrent respiratory alkalosis would be diagnosed if measured PaCO2 were LESS than expected (< 21 mm Hg, seen in early salicylate toxicity or sepsis).

options.text: Primary respiratory acidosis with a compensatory secondary metabolic acidosis
options.explanation: Metabolic compensation for respiratory acidosis increases bicarbonate; bicarbonate is never decreased to compensate for respiratory acidosis.

options.text: High anion gap metabolic acidosis with a superimposed respiratory acidosis (inadequate respiratory compensation)
options.explanation: To properly evaluate acid-base disorders: (1) Look at pH: pH 7.22 indicates acidemia; (2) Look at primary disturbance: serum HCO3- is 10 mEq/L (severely low) and anion gap is [Na+] - ([Cl-] + [HCO3-]) = 134 - (98 + 10) = 26 mEq/L (elevated > 12), confirming a primary elevated anion gap metabolic acidosis; (3) Assess respiratory compensation using Winter's formula: Expected PaCO2 = (1.5 * [HCO3-]) + 8 +/- 2. Here, Expected PaCO2 = (1.5 * 10) + 8 +/- 2 = 15 + 8 +/- 2 = 23 +/- 2 mm Hg (expected range: 21 to 25 mm Hg). The patient's measured PaCO2 is 32 mm Hg. Because the measured PaCO2 (32 mm Hg) is significantly HIGHER than the expected compensated range (21–25 mm Hg), the patient is retaining carbon dioxide (hypoventilating relative to the metabolic acidosis). This indicates a concurrent, superimposed secondary RESPIRATORY ACIDOSIS. Clinically, this typically signifies impending respiratory muscle fatigue, severe central nervous system depression from ketoacidosis, or superimposed pulmonary disease (e.g., pneumonia or severe bronchospasm), representing a critical warning sign that mechanical ventilatory support may be required.

topic: Delta-Delta Ratio in Mixed Metabolic Acid-Base Disorders
stem: A 42-year-old man with a history of alcohol use disorder is brought to the emergency department after being found unresponsive in an abandoned building. Over the preceding 4 days, he experienced intractable, repeated bilious vomiting and was unable to tolerate any oral intake. Physical examination reveals an emaciated, obtunded man with sunken eyeballs, dry mucous membranes, and poor skin turgor. Vital signs: blood pressure 84/50 mm Hg, heart rate 128/min, and respirations 22/min. Laboratory evaluation demonstrates: serum sodium 138 mEq/L, potassium 3.1 mEq/L, chloride 84 mEq/L, and bicarbonate 20 mEq/L. Serum creatinine is 2.2 mg/dL. Blood ethanol is undetectable; however, serum beta-hydroxybutyrate is markedly elevated at 8.4 mmol/L (normal: < 0.5 mmol/L), confirming alcoholic ketoacidosis. The calculated serum anion gap is 34 mEq/L (normal: 10–12 mEq/L). Calculation of the delta-delta relationship (Delta AG / Delta HCO3- = [Anion Gap - 12] / [24 - Serum HCO3-]) yields a ratio of 5.5. Which of the following mixed acid-base disorders is present in this patient?

options.text: A high anion gap metabolic acidosis combined with a concurrent metabolic alkalosis
options.explanation: In evaluating high anion gap metabolic acidosis (HAGMA), calculating the "delta-delta" ratio compares the change in anion gap to the change in serum bicarbonate: Delta AG / Delta HCO3- = (Measured AG - Normal AG [12]) / (Normal HCO3- [24] - Measured HCO3-). Under pure HAGMA stoichiometry, every 1 mEq/L of unmeasured acid (e.g., ketoacid or lactate) releases 1 H+ that consumes exactly 1 mEq/L of HCO3-, yielding a theoretical ratio of 1.0 (with a typical physiological range of 1.0 to 2.0). Here, the patient's Anion Gap is [Na+] - ([Cl-] + [HCO3-]) = 138 - (84 + 20) = 34 mEq/L. The Delta AG = 34 - 12 = +22 mEq/L. Based on this severe acid accumulation, the serum bicarbonate should have plummeted from 24 down to 24 - 22 = 2 mEq/L! Instead, the patient's measured bicarbonate is 20 mEq/L (Delta HCO3- = 24 - 20 = 4 mEq/L). The Delta AG / Delta HCO3- ratio is 22 / 4 = 5.5 (markedly > 2.0). A ratio > 2.0 indicates that the serum bicarbonate is much higher than predicted for the severe degree of ketoacidosis, proving the presence of a CONCURRENT METABOLIC ALKALOSIS. Clinically, the patient's 4 days of intractable vomiting caused massive loss of gastric hydrochloric acid (HCl), generating a prominent hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis that partially masked the profound acidemia of alcoholic ketoacidosis.

options.text: A high anion gap metabolic acidosis combined with a concurrent normal anion gap metabolic acidosis
options.explanation: A concurrent normal anion gap metabolic acidosis (e.g., diarrhea) occurs when the ratio is < 1.0 (bicarbonate drops more than the rise in anion gap), the exact opposite of this patient's findings.

options.text: A pure, uncomplicated high anion gap metabolic acidosis with appropriate buffering
options.explanation: A pure uncomplicated HAGMA has a delta ratio between 1.0 and 2.0; a ratio of 5.5 indicates a dramatic excess of bicarbonate from concurrent alkalosis.

options.text: An isolated metabolic alkalosis with an artifactual elevation in calculated anion gap
options.explanation: Beta-hydroxybutyrate is markedly elevated at 8.4 mmol/L, confirming genuine severe ketoacidosis, not an artifact.

options.text: A chronic respiratory alkalosis with full compensatory renal bicarbonate excretion
options.explanation: Respiratory alkalosis lowers bicarbonate; here the bicarbonate is elevated above the level expected for the degree of ketoacidosis.

topic: High Altitude Acclimatization 2,3-BPG and Erythropoietin Response
stem: A 26-year-old healthy male researcher travels from sea level to the Summit Station in the Peruvian Andes (elevation 4,500 meters / 14,764 feet; atmospheric barometric pressure ~430 mm Hg). Upon arrival, his arterial blood gas demonstrates: pH 7.52, PaCO2 24 mm Hg, PaO2 42 mm Hg, and HCO3- 20 mEq/L, consistent with acute hypoxia-induced hyperventilation and respiratory alkalosis. Over the subsequent 2 weeks, he remains continuously at this high altitude, allowing complete physiological acclimatization to occur. Which of the following combinations of physiological adaptations correctly describes his fully acclimatized steady state at 2 weeks compared to his baseline sea-level values?

options.text: Persistent systemic alkalemia with elevated serum bicarbonate, left-shifted hemoglobin dissociation curve, and decreased hematocrit
options.explanation: Acclimatization normalizes pH via renal bicarbonate excretion (low bicarbonate), shifts the curve rightward (via 2,3-BPG), and increases hematocrit (via EPO).

options.text: Normal arterial pH with low serum bicarbonate, elevated erythrocyte 2,3-BPG (right-shifted O2 curve), and elevated hematocrit with increased pulmonary vascular resistance
options.explanation: Acclimatization to high altitude involves sequential organ system adaptations to chronic hypobaric hypoxia: (1) Ventilation and Acid-Base: Reduced atmospheric pressure lowers ambient PO2, producing alveolar and arterial hypoxemia. Peripheral chemoreceptors (carotid bodies) trigger hyperventilation. The immediate consequence is acute respiratory alkalosis (blowing off CO2). Over 48 to 72 hours, renal compensation occurs: the kidneys downregulate bicarbonate reabsorption, excreting HCO3- in urine to restore arterial pH back toward normal (pH ~7.40 with chronically low PaCO2 and low serum HCO3-); (2) Tissue Oxygen Delivery: Erythrocytes upregulate 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate (2,3-BPG). Elevated 2,3-BPG binds deoxygenated hemoglobin, shifting the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve to the RIGHT, which promotes oxygen offloading into hypoxic peripheral tissues; (3) Hematology: Chronic renal hypoxia stabilizes Hypoxia-Inducible Factor-1alpha (HIF-1alpha), driving renal peritubular fibroblasts to secrete erythropoietin (EPO). Over 2 to 4 weeks, marrow erythropoiesis increases hematocrit and hemoglobin concentration, elevating total arterial oxygen content (CaO2); and (4) Pulmonary Hemodynamics: Generalized alveolar hypoxia triggers widespread hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction (HPV), increasing pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) and pulmonary arterial pressure, predisposing to right ventricular strain.

options.text: Marked suppression of erythropoietin secretion with low hematocrit and generalized pulmonary vasodilation
options.explanation: EPO is strongly stimulated, increasing hematocrit; hypoxia causes pulmonary vasoconstriction, never vasodilation.

options.text: Elevated PaCO2 with profound hypoventilation mediated by central medullary chemoreceptors
options.explanation: Hyperventilation persists at high altitude; PaCO2 remains chronically low due to continuous peripheral hypoxic drive.

options.text: Complete depletion of 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate in erythrocytes shifting the oxygen curve to the left
options.explanation: 2,3-BPG increases in erythrocytes during chronic altitude exposure, shifting the curve to the right to facilitate tissue oxygen extraction.

subject: Physiology
topic: Carbon Monoxide vs Methemoglobin vs Cyanide Toxicity Mechanics
stem: A 34-year-old firefighter is brought to the emergency department after being rescued from a burning industrial warehouse containing burning plastic and polyurethane furniture. He was found unconscious in a smoke-filled room. Physical examination reveals an unresponsive, comatose man with tachypnea and flushed, bright cherry-red skin, but no cutaneous burns. Vital signs: blood pressure 82/46 mm Hg, heart rate 136/min, respirations 32/min, and pulse oximetry reading 99% on a 100% non-rebreather mask. Arterial blood gas (ABG) demonstrates: pH 7.12, PaCO2 26 mm Hg, PaO2 110 mm Hg, and calculated arterial oxygen saturation (SaO2) 99%. Serum lactate is markedly elevated at 14.8 mmol/L (severe elevated anion gap metabolic acidosis). Venous blood drawn from a central venous catheter in the internal jugular vein appears strikingly bright red, with a central venous oxygen saturation (ScvO2) of 92% (normal: 65–75%). Co-oximetry reveals a carboxyhemoglobin level of 3% (normal: < 5%) and a methemoglobin level of 0.8% (normal: < 1.5%). The molecular mechanism underlying this patient’s fatal histotoxic cellular hypoxia involves the inhibition of which of the following enzymes?

options.text: Heme-bound ferrous iron (Fe2+) causing oxidation to ferric iron (Fe3+) in circulating hemoglobin
options.explanation: Oxidation of Fe2+ to Fe3+ causes methemoglobinemia (seen with dapsone, nitrites, topical benzocaine), which presents with cyanosis and chocolate-brown blood, ruled out by normal co-oximetry.

options.text: Allosteric binding of carbon monoxide to hemoglobin tetramers shifting the curve to the left
options.explanation: Carbon monoxide binds hemoglobin, reducing SaO2 and oxygen content; here carboxyhemoglobin is normal (3%) and cyanide cytochrome oxidase inhibition is present.

options.text: Mitochondrial cytochrome c oxidase (Complex IV) in the electron transport chain, blocking cellular oxygen consumption
options.explanation: The patient has acute cyanide toxicity (histotoxic hypoxia) secondary to combustion of synthetic nitrogen-containing materials (plastics, wool, polyurethane) in an enclosed fire. Cyanide (CN-) is rapidly absorbed via inhalation. Once inside cells, cyanide binds with high affinity to the ferric (Fe3+) iron atom of cytochrome a3 in mitochondrial CYTOCHROME C OXIDASE (Complex IV of the electron transport chain). This inhibits the final electron transfer from cytochrome c to molecular oxygen, completely shutting down mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation and ATP generation. Treatment is intravenous HYDROXOCOBALAMIN (which binds CN- to form non-toxic cyanocobalamin, excreted in urine) or sodium thiosulfate (which donates sulfur to rhodanese to convert cyanide to thiocyanate).

topic: Chloride Shift Hamburger Phenomenon Erythrocyte Anion Exchange
stem: In a vascular physiology laboratory investigating gas transport, blood samples are drawn simultaneously from the radial artery and the femoral vein of a healthy volunteer at rest. Biochemical analysis of the red blood cells reveals that venous erythrocytes have a significantly higher intracellular chloride ion concentration and a slightly higher mean corpuscular volume (MCV) compared to arterial erythrocytes. In the systemic capillary beds of metabolically active peripheral tissues, which of the following transport mechanisms across the erythrocyte cell membrane is directly responsible for this phenomenon (the "chloride shift" or Hamburger phenomenon)?

options.text: Active outward transport of chloride coupled to ATP hydrolysis by a P-type chloride-transporting ATPase
options.explanation: Band 3 is a passive, secondary electroneutral antiporter that does not hydrolyze ATP; furthermore, chloride enters the cell in systemic capillaries.

options.text: Sodium-potassium-2-chloride (NKCC1) cotransport driven by the basolateral sodium gradient
options.explanation: NKCC cotransporters are found in renal tubules and secretory epithelia; erythrocyte chloride shift is mediated by Band 3 (AE1).

options.text: Passive paracellular diffusion of chloride ions through tight junctions between circulating erythrocytes
options.explanation: Erythrocytes are individual circulating cells lacking tight junctions; chloride movement is strictly transcellular via the AE1 carrier.

options.text: Electroneutral exchange of intracellular bicarbonate for extracellular chloride mediated by the Band 3 (AE1) anion exchanger
options.explanation: The phenomenon described is the "chloride shift" (Hamburger phenomenon), which plays a pivotal role in carbon dioxide transport. In metabolically active peripheral tissues, CO2 diffuses across capillary endothelial membranes into erythrocytes. Inside the red blood cell, cytoplasmic carbonic anhydrase II converts CO2 and H2O into carbonic acid (H2CO3), which rapidly dissociates into H+ and bicarbonate (HCO3-). Deoxygenated hemoglobin buffers the free H+ (the Bohr effect, which facilitates oxygen unloading to tissues). As intracellular HCO3- concentration rises, the transmembrane Band 3 anion transport protein (AE1 / SLC4A1) exports HCO3- out of the erythrocyte into the plasma down its concentration gradient in an electroneutral 1:1 exchange for plasma CHLORIDE (Cl-) entering the cell. Because chloride enters the red blood cell, intracellular osmolarity increases slightly, drawing water osmotically into venous erythrocytes and causing them to swell slightly (explaining why venous hematocrit and MCV are ~1% higher than arterial values). In the pulmonary capillaries, the entire sequence reverses: dissolved HCO3- enters the RBC via Band 3, Cl- is extruded into plasma, and carbonic anhydrase converts HCO3- back to CO2 for alveolar exhalation.

options.text: Facilitated diffusion of hydrogen ions through voltage-gated proton channels paired with chloride symport
options.explanation: Protons remain inside the erythrocyte buffered by deoxyhemoglobin; bicarbonate is exported while chloride is imported.
